cues.text: A Scholar of the Kraków Academy
Born in 1390 (some sources say 1403 or 1412) at Kęty, near Oświęcim in southern Poland, John studied at the Academy of Kraków .
He distinguished himself with such affable warmth and diligence that, in the words of his early biographer Michael Miechowita, he 'won the hearts of all who came in contact with him.'
He earned degrees as bachelor, master, and doctor.
He was ordained a priest and became a professor of theology at his alma mater.
A Reluctant Parish Priest
Sent for a period to serve as parish priest at Olkusz, John found pastoral responsibility for souls a source of genuine anxiety.
After some time, he petitioned to return to academic life, resuming his post as professor of Sacred Scripture at Kraków, where he remained without interruption for the rest of his life.
A Life of Radical Charity

Despite his prestigious academic standing, John lived with striking personal austerity, distributing nearly all his income and possessions to the poor and keeping only what was strictly necessary for his own survival.
Tradition holds that he once gave away his own shoes to a beggar, explaining, when asked why he walked barefoot, that the poor man needed them more than he did.
Pilgrim to Distant Shrines
John undertook the arduous, roughly 1,800-mile pilgrimage to Jerusalem on foot, along with several pilgrimages to Rome.
He carried little more than a single sack of belongings, feats of devotion remarkable for a man already advanced in years and burdened with a demanding academic career.
A Teacher's Motto

John's own guiding principle, preserved by his early biographers, urged patience and restraint in disputes: 'Fight false opinions with patience, sweetness, and love,' rather than anger or condemnation.
This advice reflected the gentle, humble character contemporaries consistently attributed to him despite his considerable learning.
Legacy
John died at Kraków in 1473 and was buried beneath the church of St. Anne, where his relics remain venerated to this day; he was canonized in 1767.
Centuries later, the young Karol Wojtyła — the future Pope John Paul II — studied at the same Kraków Academy.
By then the Academy was the Jagiellonian University that John had served for decades, creating a quiet historical link between two of Poland's most beloved scholar-saints.
